Yeah, that was actually one of the things we went back and forth on quite a bit when we were designing the project. The original idea was very task-centric: you pick a task, say text classification or image generation or summarization, and you compare models that do that specific thing on the same hardware with the same data, so it's apples to apples. But the reality is that a huge chunk of how people actually use AI now is through these general-purpose, multitask models. Someone who wants to summarize a document isn't necessarily reaching for a small, dedicated summarization model. They're opening a chatbot built on a big generative LLM and asking it to do the summary.

So if we had left those models out, the ratings would have been kind of disconnected from real-world practice. And what we've seen in our earlier research is that these multitask generative models can use significantly more energy for the same task than a specialized model, sometimes by orders of magnitude, depending on the task. That's exactly the comparison people need to see. If you're a developer or a company deciding what to deploy, you should know that using a giant general-purpose model for something like sentiment analysis might cost a lot more energy than a fine-tuned model that does just that and does it well.

So we include them and evaluate them on the same tasks, under the same conditions, as the task-specific models. That way the star rating reflects the trade-off. It's not saying multitask models are bad. Sometimes you need that flexibility. But it makes the cost of that flexibility visible, which right now it mostly isn't. It's really about giving people the information to make a more informed choice, the same way an Energy Star label on a fridge does.

r001.rationale: The candidate says multitask and task-specific models are evaluated on the same tasks and conditions, making the energy cost of general-purpose flexibility visible so people can make informed deployment choices.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we debated a lot when we were designing the project. The whole idea of AI Energy Score is to give people a way to compare models on energy efficiency for a given task, and the cleanest way to do that is to look at models that were built for that task: a text classification model, an image generation model, a speech recognition model, and so on. So the original ten tasks we defined were all pretty well scoped.

But the reality of how people are actually deploying AI right now is that a huge fraction of it runs through these general-purpose, multitask models. People aren't necessarily pulling a dedicated summarization model off the Hub anymore; they're sending everything through a large language model and asking it to summarize, to classify, to extract, to translate, whatever. So if we only rated task-specific models, we'd be missing the models that are consuming the most energy in practice, and the ratings would end up being kind of academic.

And the comparison itself is really revealing. When you run a big general-purpose model on, say, a sentiment classification task and compare it to a small fine-tuned classifier, the gap in energy can be enormous, sometimes orders of magnitude. The multitask model will do the job, but it's bringing billions of parameters to a problem that a model a thousand times smaller can solve. So including them in the same task-based rating lets people see that trade-off directly. You can look at the leaderboard and go, okay, the general model is convenient, but for this particular use case it's a one-star model competing against five-star models.

So for us it's partly about completeness, reflecting what's actually deployed, and partly about making a point: that "one model for everything" has a real cost, and if you have a well-defined task, there's often a much more efficient way to do it. We want developers and companies to have that information when they're making architectural decisions, not just to be rating models in a vacuum.

r001.rationale: The candidate says rating multitask and task-specific models on the same task lets people see their energy trade-off directly, including the gap between a general-purpose model and a small fine-tuned model.

astra-6.text: Because we want to understand the energy implications of using one model for lots of different tasks. A multitask model can answer questions, summarize text, or classify sentiment, but that flexibility can come at an energy cost. If all you need is to classify a movie review as positive or negative, how does using a general-purpose model compare with using a model trained specifically for that task? Including both lets us make that comparison and helps people choose a model that meets their needs without using more energy than necessary.

r001.rationale: It says including both model types lets people compare a general-purpose model with one trained for a specific task, including the energy trade-off.

sol-6.1.text: We include multitask models because they’re increasingly being used for tasks that more specialized models can also do. You can ask a large language model to classify sentiment, for example, but how much energy does that use compared with a model trained specifically for sentiment analysis? Including both lets us make that comparison and helps people choose a model that fits their needs, with energy use as one of the factors.

r001.rationale: The response says including both model types enables comparison of energy use for the same task and helps people choose a model, communicating the trade-off between task-specific and general-purpose models.
